items.title: One of Europe's Oldest Cities Is Also an Amazing, Underrated Place to Eat
items.author: Adam Turner
items.summary: San Sebastián is widely regarded as Spain's culinary capital for good reason: it boasts more Michelin stars per capita than almost anywhere else on earth. But
items.text:
San Sebastián is widely regarded as Spain's culinary capital for good reason: it boasts more Michelin stars per capita than almost anywhere else on earth. But while the pretty, compact Basque seaside city is hard to beat for award-winning pintxos, another part of the country has a gastronomy hub that’s long flown under the radar.

Cádiz, considered western Europe’s oldest continually inhabited city, is often overshadowed by other Andalusian foodie hotspots, like Seville and Granada. It lies in the province of the same name, famed for sought-after bluefin tuna, sharp vinegars and world-class sherry. While celebrated chef Ángel León— the "chef of the sea"—put the province on the global stage when his experimental seafood restaurant Aponiente in nearby Puerto de Santa María became Andalusia’s first establishment to bag three Michelin stars, the wider region’s everyday food culture is just as appetising.

Santiago church in Plaza de la CatedralGetty Images

Jerez de la Frontera, with its historic bodegas, lively tabancos, and hearty tapas scene, was recently voted Spain’s capital of Gastronomy. Just down the road on the banks of the Guadalquivir, Sanlúcar de Barrameda (completing the sherry triangle alongside Jerez and El Puerto) showcases the town’s exceptionally dry manzanilla sherry and a host of well-priced restaurants serving everything from hearty Andalusian stews (guisos) to prized langoustines. Further south, Barbate has some of the world’s freshest bluefin tuna—you know it's good when around 70 percent is exported to Japan—caught using complex almadraba fishing net techniques dating back to the Phoenicians.

Yet it’s the city of Cádiz, founded by the Phoenicians as Gadir in around 1200 B.C., that is perhaps the beating heart of the province’s culinary brilliance. Old town Cádiz sits on an island-like inlet connected to mainland Spain by a long, narrow sandy peninsula. Its pastel-colored buildings, romantically decayed by the salty sea air, have earned it the nickname “Spain’s little Havana.” Beyond a constellation of top-notch restaurants, the walkable, picturesque historic center is a maze of narrow cobbled streets, Roman ruins, and a golden horseshoe-shaped inner-city beach called La Caleta.

Naturally, a city lashed by the wild Atlantic Ocean excels at one culinary discipline: fresh seafood. Central to daily life here is Mercado de Abastos, one of Spain’s oldest fresh food markets, dating back to 1838. Within its crumbling walls, veteran gaditanos (local folk known for their warmth and quick wit) haggle for shellfish, fishmongers peddle everything from fresh sardines to prized tuna, and seagulls the size of pugs circle above searching for stray offcuts.

Food lovers might prefer propping up a high table at Gadisushi, an unassuming sushi stall where the toro sashimi, prawn gyoza and scallops with miso butter are all superb. Though Cádiz’s main food market isn’t strictly seafood-focused, there’s everything from olive oil and regional cheeses (Sierra de Cádiz) to empanadas and cakes—those in the know usually opt to select a fish from Marisco Camilo and take it to nearby Bar Carrusel, where they’ll fry it for only the cover charge (order a couple of cañas and some olives to keep them sweet).

The main foodie neighborhood is La Viña, a palm-tree-lined barrio chock-a-block with busy restaurants and bars. At the heart is Casa Manteca, probably the most famous tavern in town. Rick Stein dined there on his Long Weekends, and it’s since been mentioned by every travel guide in the land—for good reason. The corner bar offers a window into old Spain: expect dusty sherry bottles, walls crammed with yellowing bullfighting photos, and classic local tapas options. Pair a sheet of chicharrones with a fino sherry, or local Payoyo goat cheese with a glass of palo cortado.

Another classic Cádiz food experience is its historic freidurías, chippies which offer cut-price fried fish wrapped in paper to locals and visitors—the battered cuttlefish chocos at Freiduría Las Flores is always a hit. Beyond these humble spots lies a scattering of sherry bars, laid-back Michelin-starred fine-dining rooms and old-world seafood institutions. Below we list a few of our favourite tables in town.

The best restaurants in Cádiz

Located on the edge of the La Viña barrio, El Faro is a tavern-turned-legendary seafood institution where punters either stand at the marbled bar for some quick-fire tapas or settle in for extravagant meals on white tablecloths in the rustic azulejos tile-clad restaurant. Don’t leave without trying the tortilla de camarones (a crispy, deep-fried prawn fritter), a famed regional delicacy here.

Address: Calle San Félix, 15, 11002 Cádiz, Spain

It took a Dutch chef to bring the first Michelin star to the city of Cádiz back in 2023. León Griffioen runs Código de Barra with his wife and maître d', Paqui Márquez. Located in the heart of the old town, the duo’s small but mighty laid-back fine dining restaurant takes diners on a culinary odyssey through the flavours of Cádiz, highlighting prime local produce like retinto beef and almadraba tuna via its two pristinely plated tasting menus.

Address: C. San Francisco, 7, 11004 Cádiz, Spain

Taberna La Manzanilla

As the name suggests, sherry is the order (literally—they only serve wine) of the day at this time-worn tavern founded in 1932. The cavernous bar smells of sweet oaky vintages and is stacked with 100-year-old wooden casks, piled high and surrounded by punters clinking glasses of amontillado and manzanilla while chewing the fat and wolfing down olives and jamón. It’s been in the same family for generations, and bartenders still chalk tabs on the bar top like the good old days. Ask politely, and they might let you take a peek in the secret sherry storage room—just don’t say we told you.

Address: C. Feduchy, 19, 11005 Cádiz, Spain

Our Spain editor's favorite places to eat in Cádiz

An icon. Taberna Casa Manteca is one of the most emblematic culinary corners in Cádiz, located in the traditional Barrio de la Viña. Founded in 1953, this historic tavern is famous for its vibrant bullfighting and flamenco atmosphere, serving outstanding local tapas on brown butcher paper surrounded by vintage photos and colourful tiles. There are two must-try specialties: Chicharrones (slow-roasted, seasoned pork belly, served cold or at room temperature, and finished with a squeeze of fresh lemon juice) and Tortillitas de Camarón (crispy, lace-like fritters made from a light batter of chickpea and wheat flour, loaded with tiny local brine shrimp). —Cynthia Martín

Address: C. Corralón de los Carros, 66, 11002 Cádiz

Casa Rafael

One of the most popular and authentic traditional taverns in Cádiz, famous for offering excellent fresh fish and seafood from the bay, homemade portion, and a carefully selected choice of local wines at very competitive prices. Located right in the heart of the historic centre, it is a spot with an extremely lively atmosphere, highly recommended to enjoy tapeo (tapas dining). —Cynthia Martín

Address: C. Periodista Emilio López, 7

Venice-born master gelato maker Carlo Guerriero leads the famous parlour La Cremería Gelato Italiano, located just steps from Victoria Beach. Guerriero, who applies his background in Industrial Chemical Engineering to scientifically balance each recipe, was officially named the number one in the world in the prestigious Gelato Festival World Ranking 2026. Also, he won second place worldwide in the grand final of the international Gelato Festival World Masters competition. He combines zero-kilometre ingredients, such as fresh milk from Conil or payoyo cheese, with gourmet elements from around the world, such as South American cocoa or authentic stone-ground Bronte pistachios. The star flavour is ‘Sherrymisú’, a reinterpretation of the famous Italian dessert but with Jerez wine. They offer vegan options, gluten-free flavours, and lactose-free alternatives. —Cynthia Martín

Address: Av. Periodista Beatriz Cienfuegos, 6

A version of this story originally appeared on Condé Nast Traveller UK.
